column1: # THE GUNS. One row per piece a captain can buy.
# Edit here, then: npm run import && npm run catalogue
# Guns fit BY THE PIECE up to what the hull bears, and `mount` says which of her counts a gun draws
# against. Broadside is counted A SIDE and mirrored, because that is how a volley fires: one
# carriage gun bought is one gun each side and two guns aboard.
# Muskets are not in this table and never will be. Small arms come off the crew she musters, with the
# swivels on her rail firing in the same volley, which is `rate()`'s business.
# damage  what one ball takes off a hull.
# reload  seconds between rounds. A mixed battery serves at the pace of its slowest piece.
# weight  what she carries for it. Enough of it takes the edge off her handling, which is the reason
# group   swivels only, and blank everywhere else. How true one throws, as a share of a musket's own
#         scatter: 1 is no better than the hands beside it, and smaller is tighter. A better swivel
#         never adds a ball to the volley; what quality buys is that the volley hits harder and lands
#         closer to where the bow points, and this is the second half of that.
# blurb   one line a captain reads.

column9: The lightest iron that is still a gun. A boat can stand it and little else can.
A small piece for a small hull. Two of them do what one real gun does.
The gun a working broadside is made of. Quick to serve and quick to reload.
A little more iron for the same port. She feels the weight but not badly.
A long barrel on a light ball. It reaches further than anything of its weight.
The upper deck gun of a ship of the line, and the main battery of a small one.
A frigate's gun. Enough iron to open a hull at the range she wants to fight.
Lower deck weight. Slow to run out, and it tells every time it goes off.
The heaviest gun that goes to sea in numbers. It breaks frames, not planks.
French weight of metal. One tier of these is most of what she can carry.
A light chaser that points where the bow points. Cheap, and it is something.
A chaser with a little more weight behind the ball.
A long barrel on the bow. Reaches further than anything else aboard.
Heavy enough to hurt a hull at the range a chase is fought at.
A frigate's chaser. Iron enough to open a stern at a distance.
Mounted on the rail and served by one hand. Clears a deck rather than holing a hull.
Cast true, so the ball goes where it was pointed. The volley lands closer to the bow.
A longer barrel on the same mount. It hits harder and throws truer than anything on the rail.
